q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂Cl is:
x: CH₃CH₂Cl has a two-carbon chain (ethane) with one chlorine, so it is chloroethane (common name ethyl chloride).

q: In the C–X bond of an alkyl halide, the carbon atom carries:
o: No charge, as the bond is non-polar
x: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the bonding electrons towards itself. Carbon becomes δ+ and the halogen δ−.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CHBrCH₃ is:
x: The chain has three carbons with Br on the middle carbon, so it is 2-bromopropane. 1-Bromopropane is CH₃CH₂CH₂Br, its positional isomer.

q: Which C–X bond is the most polar?
x: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so the electronegativity difference, and hence the polarity, is greatest in the C–F bond.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCl is:
x: The longest chain is three carbons (propane); C-2 carries both a methyl group and the chlorine, giving 2-chloro-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl chloride).

q: For the same alkyl group, the correct order of reactivity of alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution is:
x: Reactivity follows the ease of breaking the C–X bond. The C–I bond is the weakest, so iodoalkanes react fastest and fluoroalkanes slowest.

q: CHCl₃, commonly called chloroform, has the IUPAC name:
x: CHCl₃ is methane with three H atoms replaced by Cl, so it is trichloromethane. Tetrachloromethane is CCl₄.

q: Iodoalkanes are more reactive than fluoroalkanes even though the C–F bond is more polar. This is because:
o: The C–I bond is the weakest and breaks most easily
Iodine is more electronegative than fluorine
The C–I bond is the shortest C–X bond
Fluoride ion is a better leaving group than iodide ion
x: Bond strength matters more than polarity here. The long C–I bond has the lowest bond energy, so it breaks most easily; the C–F bond is very strong.

q: Which of the following is a secondary alkyl halide?
x: In 2-bromobutane the carbon bearing Br is attached to two other carbons, so it is secondary. 1-Bromobutane is primary and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary.

q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in an alkyl halide is:
x: In an alkyl halide the halogen-bearing carbon forms four single bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement, so it is sp³ hybridised.

q: 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)₂Cl, is classified as a:
x: The carbon carrying Cl is bonded to three other carbon atoms (two methyls and an ethyl), so the alkyl halide is tertiary.

q: Because of the polar C–X bond, the carbon atom bonded to the halogen in an alkyl halide is attacked mainly by:
x: The carbon is electron-deficient (δ+), so electron-rich species, nucleophiles, attack it. This is why alkyl halides typically undergo nucleophilic substitution.

q: The condensed formula of 1-bromo-2-methylpropane is:
x: Propane chain with Br on C-1 and a methyl on C-2 gives BrCH₂CH(CH₃)CH₃, i.e. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br. (CH₃)₃CBr is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

q: Which of the following is the best leaving group in nucleophilic substitution reactions of alkyl halides?
x: I⁻ is large, stable and a very weak base, and the C–I bond is weak, so iodide leaves most easily. F⁻ and OH⁻ are poor leaving groups.

q: How many structural isomers are possible for the alkyl halide C₄H₉Br?
x: There are four: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Two come from the straight chain and two from the branched chain.

q: Chloroethane can be made from ethanol with thionyl chloride, SOCl₂, in the presence of pyridine. Its main advantage over other chlorinating reagents is that:
o: It is the only reagent that converts primary alcohols
No by-products are formed at all
It gives a mixture of chloroalkanes that is easily separated
The by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases that escape, leaving the chloroalkane easy to purify
x: C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂ + HCl. Both by-products are gases, so no liquid or solid by-product (such as POCl₃ from PCl₅ or H₃PO₃ from PCl₃) must be separated. HCl/ZnCl₂ and PCl₅ also convert primary alcohols, so that option is wrong.

q: Ethanol is warmed with phosphorus tribromide, PBr₃ (made from red phosphorus and bromine). The products are:
x: 3C₂H₅OH + PBr₃ → 3C₂H₅Br + H₃PO₃: each –OH is replaced by –Br and phosphorus ends up in phosphorous acid. The HBr option is tempting from PCl₅-type reactions, which give HX, but PBr₃ gives H₃PO₃.

q: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH. The concentration of OH⁻ is doubled while [(CH₃)₃CBr] is kept the same. The rate of reaction:
x: A tertiary halide reacts by SN1: the slow step is ionisation (CH₃)₃CBr → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻, so rate = k[(CH₃)₃CBr], independent of [OH⁻]. Applying the SN2 rate law, rate = k[RX][OH⁻], gives the tempting 'doubles'.

q: In the transition state of the SN2 reaction of OH⁻ with bromomethane, CH₃Br, the central carbon atom:
o: Has lost Br completely and carries a full positive charge
Is bonded to OH and Br on the same side of the molecule
Is sp³ hybridised with four normal bonds and one lone pair
Is partly bonded to both OH and Br, which lie on opposite sides, with the three H atoms in one plane
x: In SN2 the nucleophile attacks from the back as the leaving group departs, in one step; at the transition state the C–O bond is forming and the C–Br bond breaking, on opposite sides, and the three H atoms flatten into a plane. A free carbocation belongs to SN1, the tempting mix-up; backside attack is why the product's configuration is inverted.

q: Which bromoalkane reacts fastest by the SN1 mechanism?
x: The SN1 rate depends on forming a carbocation. Three electron-donating methyl groups stabilise the tertiary (CH₃)₃C⁺ most, so (CH₃)₃CBr ionises fastest. CH₃Br is the fastest for SN2 (least crowded), the tempting reversal.

q: Methylmagnesium iodide, CH₃MgI, reacts with water. The organic product is:
x: The CH₃ group is carbanion-like and takes H⁺ from water: CH₃MgI + H₂O → CH₄ + Mg(OH)I. This is why Grignard reagents must be made in dry ether. Methanol is tempting by analogy with hydrolysis of alkyl halides, but no C–O bond forms.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide reacts with methanal, HCHO, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The alcohol formed is:
x: CH₃⁻ adds to the carbonyl carbon of HCHO, giving CH₃CH₂OMgBr; hydrolysis gives CH₃CH₂OH. Methanal always gives a primary alcohol with one more carbon. Propan-2-ol comes from ethanal and 2-methylpropan-2-ol from propanone, the usual mix-ups.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide reacts with ethanal, CH₃CHO, followed by hydrolysis with dilute acid. The product is:
x: CH₃ adds to the carbonyl carbon, which already carries one CH₃ and one H, so the product after hydrolysis is CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, a secondary alcohol. Propan-1-ol would need the new group on the end carbon; aldehydes other than methanal give secondary alcohols.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide reacts with propanone, CH₃COCH₃, followed by hydrolysis with dilute acid. The product is:
x: The carbonyl carbon of propanone carries two CH₃ groups; adding a third and then –OH gives (CH₃)₃COH, a tertiary alcohol. Ketones give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents. Propan-2-ol is tempting if the new methyl is forgotten (that is the reduction product).

q: Which pair of reagents, followed by hydrolysis with dilute acid, gives butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
x: Cutting butan-2-ol at the carbinol carbon leaves CH₃CHO plus an ethyl group, so C₂H₅MgBr + CH₃CHO works. CH₃MgBr + propanone gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol (same C₄ count, the tempting slip), CH₃MgBr + methanal gives ethanol and C₂H₅MgBr + methanal gives propan-1-ol.

q: Ethylmagnesium bromide, C₂H₅MgBr, reacts with dry carbon dioxide and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The organic product is:
x: The ethyl group adds to the carbon of CO₂, giving C₂H₅COOMgBr; acid hydrolysis gives C₂H₅COOH. The acid has one more carbon than the Grignard reagent, so ethanoic acid (no extra carbon) is the tempting slip.

q: 14.2 g of iodomethane is converted completely into CH₃MgI, which is then treated with excess water. What volume of methane is formed at STP? (I = 127; molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: Mr of CH₃I = 12 + 3 + 127 = 142, so 14.2 g = 0.1 mol. One CH₃I gives one CH₃MgI, which gives one CH₄, so 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. Treating the mole ratio as 2 : 1 gives 1.12 dm³.

q: Methylmagnesium bromide is added to ethanol. A gas is given off. The gas is:
x: Ethanol has an acidic O–H hydrogen; the CH₃ group of the Grignard reagent takes it: CH₃MgBr + C₂H₅OH → CH₄ + C₂H₅OMgBr. The alkane formed always comes from the Grignard alkyl group, so ethane (from the alcohol's ethyl) is the tempting slip.

q: In a Grignard reagent such as CH₃CH₂MgBr, the carbon atom bonded to magnesium:
o: Carries a partial negative charge and acts as a nucleophile
Carries a partial positive charge and acts as an electrophile
Is uncharged because the C–Mg bond is non-polar
x: Magnesium is less electronegative than carbon (about 1.2 versus 2.5), so the C–Mg bond is polarised C^δ−–Mg^δ+. The carbon behaves like a carbanion and attacks electron-poor carbon, such as a carbonyl carbon. Students who carry over the C^δ+ of alkyl halides choose the electrophile option.

q: A carbonyl compound X reacts with ethylmagnesium bromide, and hydrolysis of the product gives 3-methylpentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. X is:
x: Removing one ethyl group from the carbinol carbon leaves CH₃–C(=O)–CH₂CH₃, butanone; a ketone is needed because the product is a tertiary alcohol. Pentan-3-one would give 3-ethylpentan-3-ol, propanone gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol, and propanal gives the secondary alcohol pentan-3-ol.
